*Gaia Smith & Alice Thompson*

## 1. Introduction

**1.1 Significance of this archaeological find and Gela**

The historic Gela, in Sicily Italy has been a treasure trove of archaeological finds for generations. This ancient city was strategically positioned at the crux of major maritime trade routes, which made it a populous and successful trading port [@Angelucci2026]. Consequently, ships looking to trade goods like pottery, metals, and grain have traveled, and sunk, around Gela for centuries.

A shipwreck off the coast continues to provide significant archaeological finds to this day. This discovery dates back to 1988 [@nuttersworldGelaWreck], where it was first stumbled upon by divers near Bulala beach. We are exploring one of the most significant finds from this wreck; A veritable hoard of the fabled metal, Orichalcum.

The discovery of 40 orichalcum ingots in 2017 was a monumental one. There had never been a discovery of this quantity in one place anywhere in the world. There was also evidence of consistent casting processes, with overall similarities suggesting a rudimentary mold production. This was likely a hole dug in the ground and molten alloy was poured in the indentation to solidify. The morphology of the found ingots suggested cast-diverse technologies.

**2.2 What is orichalcum?**

Orichalcum is defined as a copper alloy with zinc content as the principal components. A widely varying quantity of lead and tin among other trace elements are expected. There is no consistent proportion to the amount of copper and zinc found, but the overall composition and relative amounts of principal elemental components can be used to deduce the rough date and origin of a sample. The modern day equivalent is brass.

**2.3 Summary of Collection Techniques**

In the initial analysis of the orichalcum ingots, X-Ray Fluorescence (XRF) spectroscopy via a portable spectrometer [@Caponetti2017-sc] was used. The subject paper includes that data and further investigates the composition of each ingot using more invasive and refined elemental analysis.

For further testing, and the subject of this paper, @Caponetti2017-fd chose to test elemental compositions using Inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-OES) and Inductively coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy (ICP-MS) of each of the 38 orichalcum ingots. ICP-OES was used to obtain measures for the primary elements above 1000 parts per million (PPM) while ICP-MS was used for the more difficult to measure trace elements below 1000 PPM. Both techniques are destructive and require the extraction of \~20mg of the ingots by drilling a micro-well into each ingot to obtain material for testing.

**2.4 Scope of This Multivariate Analysis**

This multivariate analysis includes manipulations of the data collected from the ICP-OES and ICP-MS chemometric analysis, it does not include the data about physical characteristics of the ingots or any correlation analysis of those variables.

We have chosen to reuse data because the orichalcum ingot archaeological find near Gela, Italy is a literally one of a kind find, we do not have the resources or the belief that it would be ethical to conduct excessive destructive testing on artifacts that may never be found again. Therefore, we have used @Caponetti2017-sc ICP-OES and ICP-MS data of 38 orichalcum ingots.

Our goal is to create and present a comprehensive, comprehensible, reproducible, and replicable multivariate analysis of the data obtained from chemometric elemental analysis of 38 orichalcum ingots to determine if there is coherent clustering between samples that are consistent with different distances and linkages.

We will be excluding the Cu/Zn ratio variable in the source table as we chose to analyse the linkage of all elements between each other, not between Cu/Zn ratios and other elements

## 3. EDA

**3.1 Analysing raw data**

Using R, summary statistics (\@sum-stat) were created from table 1 and initial observations were made. We found that concentrations for each element varied greatly in range and skew, where skew in this case is distance between mean and median.

```{r, Summary Statistics ,echo = FALSE}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6
#| label: sum-stat

Element_order <- colnames(as.data.frame(Ingots_F_no[, -1]))

Ingots_sum <- Ingots_F_no[, -1] |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = everything(),
    names_to = "Element",
    values_to = "Concentration"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    Element = factor(Element, levels = Element_order)
  ) |>
  group_by(Element) |>
  summarise(
    Mean = mean(Concentration, na.rm = TRUE),
    SD = sd(Concentration, na.rm = TRUE),
    Min = min(Concentration, na.rm = TRUE),
    Q1 = quantile(Concentration, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE),
    Median = median(Concentration, na.rm = TRUE),
    Q3 = quantile(Concentration, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE),
    Max = max(Concentration, na.rm = TRUE),
    IQR = IQR(Concentration, na.rm = TRUE),
    Kurtosis = kurtosis(Concentration, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

knitr::kable(
  Ingots_sum, 
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Summary Statistics of Table 1", 
  format = "pipe")

```

The elements Sb, As, Sn, Li, Sr, and Ba all show strong positive skews, numerous other elements show weaker skews. Cu and Zn are roughly symmetric. Ranges vary greatly with many magnitude differences between the 'percentage based' vs the 'ppm' elements (where percentage is \~10\^4 more then ppm of the same value assuming the 2 measurement techniques are equally accurate) and between trace element ranges (Rb having a minimum of 0.03ppm while Ni has a maximum of 683ppm), and between the different samples vs same element (I.e. Sr has a minimum of 0.08ppm and a maximum of 15.10ppm which is over 180 times move than the minimum) these characteristics hint that a data transformation may be appropriate to increase interpretability.

@Caponetti2017-fd observed that samples S13, S25, and S38 were potential outliers due to various unusual element concentrations which we also noted. We also found that S22, S18, and S17 appear to have high Sr content (15.1ppm, 11.8ppm, 7.27ppm respectively, compared to a median of 0.42ppm) while S28, S22, and S19 have high Ba content (4.59ppm, 3.61ppm, 3.37ppm respectively, compared to a median of 0.28ppm).

Data clustering analysis may find that these groupings of samples cluster together in similar groups, furthering @Caponetti2017-fd, who claimed that trace element analysis could be used to differentiate providence of orichalcum alloy production.

![Notch Boxplot](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/luke8471/STAT394-GROUP-3/main/Figures/notchbox.png)

Ni (nickel) had the widest interquartile range of 90.00, indicating the greatest variation among the samples, while Sb (antimony) shows the largest total range, likely driven by sample 13's recorded Sb being magnitudes larger than any of the other samples.

Due to the fact the data was recorded at different scales (percentage and PPM) and obvious outliers, log transformation and scaling were the next logical steps.

**3.2 QQ-plots & Henze-Zirkler Test For Multivariate Normality**

We first created and visually assessed the QQ-normal plots of table 1 to see if data transformation would be appropriate to manage potential outliers and standardisation issues.

![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/luke8471/STAT394-GROUP-3/main/Figures/QQ_all.png)

As this was before there was any scaling performed, we opted to display the elements individually to better display each elements influence.

##### Primary Elements

Cu roughly follows the normal QQ-line, indicating it may follow a normal distribution. Fe and Pb are similarly distributed to Cu, but show slight deviation from QQ-line in the upper and lower tails. Zn has clear deviation from the QQ-line in the upper tail.

##### Trace Elements

Ag, Co, and Ni roughly follow the QQ-line indicating some evidence for normality. All other trace elements have blatant deviations from the normal line, particularly in the upper tail, likely due to previously discussed potential outliers. The relatively small sample size of 38, the tiny concentrations relative to the main elements, and the small amount of material taken/used for this material analysis technique are all 3 factors that could and likely would be influencing the data.

#### Data Transformation

We tried a simple log transformation witch resulted in a few zero values which was of some concern, as log(0) is undefined and can influence towards non-normality in multivariate data, particularly in small datasets like this one. We also had negative values. These were not an issue because we later chose metrics which are calculated from coordinate distances for clustering which can handle negative values.

Zero values were compensated for by instead transforming using log($\mathcal x$ + 1), where $\mathcal{x}$ is our data.

Henze-Zirkler test established if there was preliminary evidence for multivariate normality.

```{r, echo = FALSE}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6

#log transform data

logIngots1 <- log(as.matrix(Ingots_F_no[-1,-1] + 1))

#print(logIngots1)

#knitr::kable(logIngots1,
             #caption = "Log(x + 1) Transformed Data",
             #format = "pipe")

```

![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/luke8471/STAT394-GROUP-3/main/Figures/QQ_allnorm.png)

The QQ-plot of the log($\mathcal x$ + 1) showed slight improvement overall. Multiple trace elements which had big upper skews now follow the theoretical line better with As, V, and Cr in particular following the theoretical line better.

There is still evidence of some elements not following assumptions of normality with Sr being the most prominent example, however, after the log($\mathcal x$ + 1) transformation and considering the small sample size of the data set and most elements roughly following the line. We concluded that the assumption of normality would need further testing to evaluate, but appears to hold.

![Notch Boxplot](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/luke8471/STAT394-GROUP-3/main/Figures/notchboxnorm.png)

Ni (nickel) wen from widest to having an interquartile range smaller then the average, while Sb (antimony) went from largest range to again becoming much closer to the average. Overall we can clearly see that the standardisation and log($\mathcal x$ + 1) transformation have greatly added in the interpretability of our EDA graphs. We note that Sr appears to have 4 unusual values/outliers.

```{r, echo = FALSE}

HZoriginal <- MVN::mvn(data = logIngots1, mvn_test = "hz")

hz_table <- HZoriginal$multivariate_normality

knitr::kable(
  hz_table,
  digits = 2,
  caption = "Henze-Zirkler Test For Multivariate Normality"
)
```

The Henze-Zirkler test stipulates

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal{H}_0 :& 
\text{ The data follow a multivariate normal distribution},
\\
\mathcal{H}_1 :& 
\text{ The data do not follow a multivariate normal distribution}.
\end{aligned}
$$

This generated a p-value=0.069, suggesting that there is insufficient evidence to reject that the data follow a multivariate normal distribution. However, the QQ-plot shows many variables with evidence of non-normality and/or significant outliers that we decided further testing was warranted before determining if multivariate normality is an appropriate statistical assumption.

Data manipulation by Median Absolute Deviation (MAD) was determined to be the next best step towards multivariate analysis.

**3.3 MAD**

MAD was used because it is a robust, outlier-resistant, measure of variability. The log($\mathcal x$ +1) transformation somewhat fixed the skew and pulled the outliers in, but did not eliminate their mathematical influence. Interpreting variation in the data using the standard deviation which is highly affected by unusually high/low values or outliers would be statistically unsound.

```{r transformations-mad, echo=FALSE}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6

#Calculate medians and MAD for each column:
median <- apply(logIngots1[,-1], 2, median)
mad <- apply(logIngots1[,-1], 2, mad)


#print(median/mad)
#mad

MAD_summary <- as.data.frame(logIngots1) |>
  pivot_longer(
    everything(),
    names_to = "Element",
    values_to = "Concentration"
      ) |>
  group_by(Element) |>
  summarise(
    Median = median(Concentration),
    MAD = mad(Concentration),
    Skewness = moments::skewness(Concentration),
    Kurtosis = moments::kurtosis(Concentration),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

knitr::kable(
  MAD_summary,
  caption = "Median Absolute Deviation Summary Table",
  digits = 2,
  format = "pipe"
)

```

From observed some massive deviations, as expected.

Variance because MAD\>SD robustness

Outliers MAD/median

Next the robust Z score was used to identify outliers that were candidates for removal. For our cutoff, we went with @Leys2013-cr recommendation, who argued that the MAD is the most robust scale measure under contamination and recommend a median plus or minus 2.5 time MAD rule for outlier detection.

```{r outliers, echo=FALSE}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6

#Compute the robust z-scores:
z <- scale(logIngots1[,-1], center = median, scale = mad)

#Flag observations where any variable exceeds the threshold
outliers <- apply(abs(z) > 2.5, 1, any)

#list(outliers)

z_scores <- as.data.frame(scale(logIngots1[, ]))

# View the rows flagged as outliers
invisible(summary(logIngots1[outliers,]))

Ingots_clean <- logIngots1[rowSums(abs(z_scores) > 2.5) == 0, ]

```

What is after we have "cleaned" up the outliers our \|z\| \> 2.5 rule removes samples 13, 25, and 38 which is exactly the sample ingots that Caponetti et al. set aside as their G4 group. Samples 7, 13 ,14 ,17, 19, 21, 22, and 28 were also removed using the same cut off.

{should probably explain why cutting out 11 samples will be good for the rest of our analysis, something along the line of outliers, terrible samples and low sample quality}.

**2.4 Multivariate normal distribution**

```{R Henze Zirkler, echo=FALSE, warning = FALSE}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6

#HZ test on OG data, which also rejects null.

HZoriginal <- MVN::mvn(data = Ingots_F_no, mvn_test = "hz")
cat("Henze_Zirkler Test Results:\n")
print(HZoriginal$multivariate_normality)

#Henze-Zirkler test on cleaned data?
#Non-negative functional distance that measures between two distribution functions. If data
#is MVN, the test statistic HZ is approximately lognormally distributed. It calculates mean,
#variance, and smoothness parameter. Mean and variance are then log-normalised and p-value
#is estimated.
#@MISC{noauthor_undated-de,
#  howpublished = "\url{https://www.rdocumentation.org/packages/MVN/versions/5.8/topics/hzTest}",
#  note         = "Accessed: 2026-9-15"
#}

HZ <- MVN::mvn(data = Ingots_clean, mvn_test = "hz")

cat("Henze_Zirkler Test Results:\n")
print(HZ$multivariate_normality)
```

Conducting the Henze Zirkler test for both the un-transformed data (p-value \<0.001) and the transformed data (p-value 0.055) we can reject the null hypotheses and conclude that the data is only not-normal when it is not-transformed and outliers remain. After log($\mathcal x$ + 1) transformation and outlier removal using MAD, we can no longer safely reject the null hypotheses and have weak evidence (due to the p-value being barely above the cut off) that the processed data can be assumed to be multivariate normal.

**2.5 Correlation plots before and after**

![](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/luke8471/STAT394-GROUP-3/main/Figures/correlation_matrix.png)

![Correlation matrix of log-Transformed Data](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/luke8471/STAT394-GROUP-3/main/Figures/correlation_matrix_log.png)

Many of the element to element correlations change in degree and direction between the raw data and log(x + 1)-transformed data correlation matrices. Because Pearson correlations are not robust to changes due to outliers/heavily skewed data, we believe the transformed data correlation plot is a more accurate plot to make interpretations from.

Simple observations include a strong-positive correlation between Sb-As, Fe-Co, Ag-Bi, V-Cr, Cr-Rb, Cu-Bi, Cu-Ag, Sb-Cd, all of these pairs have an above 0.8 correlation value. Compared to the positive, strong-negative correlation can be found between Cd-Sn at \~-0.8 correlation value, with a multiple pairs having a somewhat strong-negative correlation in the negative 0.7 to -0.8 range. Interestingly the elements needed to create orichalchum/brass do not have strong correlations with one another.

This is a positive sign that the robustness of the transformation, i.e removing some of the outliers demonstrates their influence on the raw data.

Given the uncertainty about multivariate normality and the presence of negative values in our transformed data, a linear data analysis was chosen over a primary component analysis.

## 4. LDA

**4.1 PAM**

We started by performing a PAM (Partitioning Around Medoids) analysis

```{r LDA, echo=FALSE}
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 6

#need to find optimal silhouette width
ICN <- as.data.frame(Ingots_clean[,-1])

ICN[] <- lapply(ICN, as.numeric)

scaled <- scale(ICN)

sil_avg <- numeric(25)

LDA_K <- data.frame(k = 2:26, avg_silhouette = sil_avg)

pam_sum_tab <- data.frame()

for (k in 2:25) {
  
  PAM_fit <- cluster::pam(scaled, k)
  
  sizes <- table(PAM_fit$clustering)
  
  pam_sum_tab <- rbind(
    pam_sum_tab,
    data.frame(
      k = k,
      Avg_Silhouette = round(PAM_fit$silinfo$avg.width, 3),
      Smallest_Cluster = min(sizes),
      Largest_Cluster = max(sizes),
      Cluster_Sizes = paste(sizes, collapse = ", ")
    )
  )
}

pam <- pam(Ingots_clean, k = 3)

cluster <- pam$clustering

#for (k in 2:25) {
  #PAM_fit <- pam(scaled, k)
  #sil_avg[k - 1] <- PAM_fit$silinfo$avg.width
#}

top_pam <- pam_sum_tab |>
  arrange(desc(Avg_Silhouette)) |>
  slice(1:5)

knitr::kable(
  top_pam,
  caption = "Top five cluster choices ranked by average silhouette width."
)

```

The silhouette value/metric is a measurement of the quality of a clustering. between -1 and 1. The data reports the optimal silhouette width as 5, with 0.6496032, indicating some. There are several other clustering values with a reported similar quality.

Due to the ambiguous clustering, we opted to perform more cluster analyses to determine if this was a good fit.

MANHATTAN NOT EUCLEDIAN.

## 5. Linkage Analysis

Hierarchical cluster using Manhattan Distance as a measure. Chosen because it is more robust to outliers then Eucledian.

![Dendrogram](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/luke8471/STAT394-GROUP-3/main/Figures/dendrogram.png)

Cophenetic correlation coefficient ranges between -1 to 1, with a value of 1 indicating a perfect fit between the clusters and the data. A value of 0.798 means that the clustering is a fairly good fit. CCC can be used to compare between clustering methods.

We can see which sample pairs are more similar to one another, then to other sample pairs, for example samples 5 and 8 are more similar to one another then either is too the rest of the yellow cluster. We can also see for example that sample 32 is most similar to the grouping of samples 31, 3, 10, and 29 then to any of those samples individually.

## 6. Cluster Analysis

##### **6.1 UMAP Projection**

Given the low cophenetic correlation from the linkage analysis and the ambiguous silhouette width associated with the chosen k = 3 from the PAM analysis, we performed a UMAP projection to better visualise the clustering.

![UMAP](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/luke8471/STAT394-GROUP-3/main/Figures/UMAP.png)

The UMAP projection shows clear overlap groupings....

**6.2 Fuzzy Analysis**

As the fourth and final method of clustering, we performed a Fuzzy analysis.

```{r, echo = FALSE}
Fuzzy_k <- FKM.med(scaled, k = 3, m = 2)

#silhouettes

#Table of Fuzzy_K$U:
knitr::kable(Fuzzy_k$U,
             caption = "Fuzzy K Silhouettes Clusterings",
             format = "pipe")

```

![Fuzzy Membership Certainty](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/luke8471/STAT394-GROUP-3/main/Figures/Fuzzy.png)

The graph of Fuzzy Membership Certainty shows that the majority of our observations are near ambiguous in there assigned groupings.

Picks by median centrality, determines closest group and percentage it belongs in said group.

## 5. Results

```{r, echo = FALSE}
#creating tables to visually compare results from PAM, H cluster, UMAP, Fuzzy.

# PAM

k <- umap(scaled)
PamMan <- pam(scaled, k = 3, metric = "manhattan")

pam_fit <- pam(scaled, k = 3)
pam_size <- table(pam_fit$clustering)
pam_avg_sil <- pam_fit$silinfo$avg.width
pam_clust <- pam_fit$clustering

# Hierarchical

d <- dist(scaled, method = "manhattan")
HiMan <- hclust(d, method = "average")

h_clust <- cutree(HiMan, k = 3)
hclust_size <- table(h_clust)
hclust_sil <- silhouette(h_clust, d)
hclust_avg_sil <- mean(hclust_sil[, "sil_width"])

#UMAP clustering
#PamMan

umap_size <- table(PamMan$clustering)
umap_avg_sil <- PamMan$silinfo$avg.width
umap_clust <- PamMan$clustering

# Fuzzy
```

## 6. Discussion

@Caponetti2017-sc determined 3 distinct groupings of ingots, which provides evidence of a scarce and highly prized alloy being manufactured in one place at one time. This was determined with the added variable of the physical form of the ingots.

Our results

The ICP-OE and ICP-MS chemometric techniques require a small amount of material to be sacrificed in order to obtain a full range of the elemental composition of each ingot.

XRF is a portable, non-invasive method of getting accurate readings within a certain range of elements (find that bit again). The ICP-OE and ICP-MS chemometric techniques require a small amount of material to be sacrificed in order to obtain a full range of the elemental composition of each ingot.

@Caponetti2017-fd performed chemoanalysis to determine the trace elements of these orichalcum ingots. Using this data, they determined correlation between the observed different features and the composition to group the ingots into their appropriate cluster. This is an extension from a fledgling study by the same author, where they performed a less invasive XRF (X-Ray Fluorescence) spectroscopy of the ingots, a non-distructive test that can be performed in the field.

Their motivation was to create a starting point for giving insight into archaeometric study of the orichalcum ingots regarding their origin and manufacture technologies.

Our study also has the same motivations. We aim to provide a high level data analysis to provide a detailed, and logical, path to a linkage analysis.
